parts.visual:
Blockbuster Video had thousands of stores and billions in profit. Netflix was a tiny startup mailing DVDs. Why didn't Blockbuster crush Netflix?

The Dilemma:
1. The Cash Cow: Blockbuster made its money from charging 'Late Fees' when people forgot to return VHS tapes.
2. The Disruption: Netflix had no late fees. To beat Netflix, Blockbuster would have to eliminate its own late fees, instantly destroying its own massive profits.
3. The Paralysis: Great companies fail because they logically refuse to destroy their current profitable business model to chase an unproven, lower-margin new technology.
parts.audio: The Innovator's Dilemma, coined by Clayton Christensen, explains why dominant companies fail. They refuse to invest in disruptive technology because doing so would destroy the massive profits of their current business model.

questions.question: Kodak literally invented the first digital camera in 1975. Why did they hide it in a closet and eventually go bankrupt when digital cameras took over?
options: Because digital cameras were too heavy.

The Innovator's Dilemma. Kodak made 80% of its money selling chemical film. If they pushed digital cameras, nobody would buy film anymore. They chose to protect their Cash Cow instead of embracing the future.
questions.correct_answer: The Innovator's Dilemma. Kodak made 80% of its money selling chemical film. If they pushed digital cameras, nobody would buy film anymore. They chose to protect their Cash Cow instead of embracing the future.
questions.explanation: If you don't cannibalize your own business, a startup will do it for you.

questions.question: Listen to the Corporate Board. Why are they rejecting the CEO's proposal to build electric cars?
questions.tts_text: We make $10,000 profit on every gas-powered truck we sell. Electric cars have terrible margins, and our best customers don't even want them. Why should we waste billions on a losing product?
options: Because the Board is environmentally friendly.

They are making a perfectly rational, logical business decision based on current data—which is exactly how the Innovator's Dilemma traps companies. They listen to their current customers instead of looking at the future.
Because they like the smell of gas.
questions.correct_answer: They are making a perfectly rational, logical business decision based on current data—which is exactly how the Innovator's Dilemma traps companies. They listen to their current customers instead of looking at the future.
questions.explanation: Disruptive technology almost always starts out as a 'worse' product with terrible profit margins, making it invisible to massive corporations until it's too late.

questions.question: What is 'Sustaining Innovation' vs 'Disruptive Innovation'?
options: Sustaining innovation makes an existing product 5% better (a sharper razor blade). Disruptive innovation creates an entirely new market, often starting as a cheap, low-quality alternative that eventually takes over.
questions.correct_answer: Sustaining innovation makes an existing product 5% better (a sharper razor blade). Disruptive innovation creates an entirely new market, often starting as a cheap, low-quality alternative that eventually takes over.
questions.explanation: Incumbents win at sustaining innovation. Startups win at disruptive innovation.

questions.question: How did Apple survive the Innovator's Dilemma when they launched the iPhone?
options: Steve Jobs was willing to ruthlessly cannibalize his own Cash Cow. He knew the iPhone (which played music) would instantly destroy the iPod business, but he did it anyway.
questions.correct_answer: Steve Jobs was willing to ruthlessly cannibalize his own Cash Cow. He knew the iPhone (which played music) would instantly destroy the iPod business, but he did it anyway.
questions.explanation: Only a founder with absolute dictatorial control can force a company to destroy its most profitable product on purpose.
